label: Aggregates / construction materials

capacity.note: Capacity is local, not national. Rock is abundant but freight is roughly a third of delivered cost, so the economic haul radius is near 25 miles and each quarry serves its own market. National share is close to meaningless; what matters is being #1 or #2 within the radius, and how many years of permitted reserves sit inside it.

pricing.note: Pricing has held through a volume downturn, which is the whole thesis. Crushed-stone PPI is +6.0% year over year and VMC's freight-adjusted price is +4.3% to $21.98/ton, while single-family starts are -15.7%. Freight-adjusted is the only comparable measure: unadjusted ASP tracks diesel, not pricing power.

regulatory.note: Zoning and permitting are simultaneously the moat and the tail risk. New quarries near a growing metro are close to un-permittable, which protects incumbents and deepens the moat over time; the same process can contest a renewal on one critical site, and a company-average reserve life hides that. Aggregates M&A also draws antitrust divestiture conditions.

scope_note: A thesis industry, not a horizon one: nothing here is forming or transitioning. The edge is that the structure does not change -- freight localises the market, permitting keeps new supply out, and unit profitability compounds through cycles. Demand splits between residential (cyclical, currently weak) and public infrastructure (counter-cyclical, currently +4.5%); federal surface-transportation reauthorisation is the largest swing factor and has no automated source.
